```{python}
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker

# Rendering runs from article/, but running cells in the editor starts wherever
# the kernel does (usually the project root), so find article/ either way.
ARTICLE_DIR = next(d for d in (Path.cwd(), Path.cwd() / "article", Path.cwd().parent / "article")
                   if (d / "article_lib.py").exists())
sys.path.insert(0, str(ARTICLE_DIR))

import article_lib as L
from article_lib import LEVEL_LABEL_ORDER, pct, num

L.apply_style()

# --- Position players -------------------------------------------------------------
dfc = L.load_fielding_plays(refresh)
f_agg, f_q = L.qualify_fielding(dfc)
f_dist = L.level_distribution(f_q)
f_trans = L.adjacent_transitions(f_q, ["player_code", "position"])
f_models = L.transition_models(f_trans, min_n=30)
f_pers = L.persistence_table(f_trans)
f_year, f_cohort, f_minors = L.mlb_cohort(
    f_q, L.first_mlb_appearance(dfc, "game_date"), percentile_within="position")
f_age = L.add_age(f_q, L.load_birth_dates(refresh))
qp = f_q[f_q["position"] != "catcher"].copy()
pairs = L.position_pairs(qp)
moves = L.position_moves(qp)
f_age_change, f_age_pairs, f_age_effects = L.aging_curve(f_age)
f_age_change_z, _, _ = L.aging_curve(f_age, n_boot=0, measure="z")
f_age_profile = L.age_profile(f_age)

# --- Catchers (framing) ------------------------------------------------------
c_agg, c_q = L.qualify_framing(L.load_framing_level_agg(refresh))
c_dist = L.level_distribution(c_q)
c_trans = L.adjacent_transitions(c_q, ["player_code"])
c_models = L.transition_models(c_trans, min_n=20)
c_pers = L.persistence_table(c_trans)
c_year, c_cohort, c_minors = L.mlb_cohort(c_q, L.first_mlb_appearance(c_agg, "first_game"))

# --- Catchers (throwing) ---------------------------------------------------
throws = L.load_catcher_throwing(refresh)
t_all, t_q = L.qualify_throwing(throws)
throw_first_year, throw_last_year = int(throws["year"].min()), int(throws["year"].max())
split = L.catcher_value_split(c_q, t_all)
split_by = split.set_index("level_label")
mlb_split = split_by.loc["MLB"]
share_lo, share_hi = pct(split["throwing_share"].min()), pct(split["throwing_share"].max())
share_avg = pct((split["throwing_share"] * split["catcher_seasons"]).sum() / split["catcher_seasons"].sum())
corr_lo, corr_hi = num(split["corr"].min()), num(split["corr"].max())
steal_fx, steal_n = L.steal_model(throws)
cs_grid, grid_n = L.caught_stealing_grid(throws)
cs_arm, arm_n = L.caught_stealing_by_arm(throws)
grid_best = cs_grid.iloc[0]["caught_rate"]    # fastest pop, quickest delivery
grid_worst = cs_grid.iloc[-1]["caught_rate"]  # slowest pop, slowest delivery
delivery = L.throw_runs_by_delivery(throws)
delivery_quick, delivery_slow = delivery["runs_per_attempt"].iloc[0], delivery["runs_per_attempt"].iloc[-1]
t_trans = L.adjacent_transitions(t_q, ["player_code"])
t_models = L.transition_models(t_trans, min_n=20)
t_keep_pct = pct(t_models["slope"].mean())
t_pers = L.persistence_table(t_trans)
cs_rate_all = throws["caught"].mean()
pop_levels = L.pop_time_by_level(throws)
pop_carry_slope, pop_carry_r, pop_carry_n = L.pop_time_carry(throws)
pop_repeat_r, pop_repeat_n = L.pop_time_repeat(throws)
frame_throw_ratio = (split["framing_sd"] / split["throwing_sd"]).mean()
pop_low, pop_mlb = pop_levels.iloc[0], pop_levels.loc[L.LEVEL_NUM["mlb"]]
pop_low_label = L.LEVEL_LABEL_ORDER[int(pop_levels.index[0]) - 1]
pop_years = sorted(int(y) for y in throws.loc[throws["catcher_pop_time"].notna(), "year"].unique())
pop_year_text = str(pop_years[0]) if len(pop_years) == 1 else f"{pop_years[0]}–{pop_years[-1]}"

# --- Who moves up: seasons old enough that players had 2+ more seasons to move
PROMOTION_WINDOW = 2
promo_last_start = int(dfc["year"].max()) - PROMOTION_WINDOW
f_promo_rows, f_promo = L.promotion_outcomes(f_q, f_agg, promo_last_start)
c_promo_rows, c_promo = L.promotion_outcomes(c_q, c_agg, promo_last_start)


def promo_summary(summary):
    p = summary.set_index("starting_group")
    return (pct(p.loc["Bottom 20%", "moved_up"]), pct(p.loc["Top 20%", "moved_up"]),
            pct(p.loc["Bottom 20%", "reached_mlb"]), pct(p.loc["Top 20%", "reached_mlb"]))


f_promo_bottom, f_promo_top, f_mlb_bottom, f_mlb_top = promo_summary(f_promo)
c_promo_bottom, c_promo_top, c_mlb_bottom, c_mlb_top = promo_summary(c_promo)
_, t_promo = L.promotion_outcomes(t_q, t_all, promo_last_start)
t_promo_bottom, t_promo_top, _, _ = promo_summary(t_promo)

# --- Level-to-level translation (each player's combined record at each level)
TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS = {"fielders": 30, "catchers": 20}
f_records = L.level_records(f_agg, ["player_code", "position"], L.FIELDING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES)
f_tr = L.translation_table(f_records, ["player_code", "position"], TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["fielders"])
f_tr_by_pos = {
    L.POSITION_LABELS[pos]: L.translation_table(f_records[f_records["position"] == pos], ["player_code", "position"],
                                                TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["fielders"])
    for pos in L.SPECTRUM_ORDER
}
c_tr = L.translation_table(
    L.level_records(c_agg, ["player_code"], L.FRAMING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES),
    ["player_code"], TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["catchers"])
t_tr = L.translation_table(
    L.level_records(t_all, ["player_code"], L.THROWING_MIN_ATTEMPTS),
    ["player_code"], TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["catchers"])
swaps = L.swap_table(qp, TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["fielders"])
up_down = L.up_down_comparison([("Position players", f_q, ["player_code", "position"]),
                                ("Catcher framing", c_q, ["player_code"]),
                                ("Catcher throwing", t_q, ["player_code"])])

# --- Numbers quoted in the text ------------------------------------------
last_game = dfc["game_date"].max()
data_through = f"{last_game:%B} {last_game.day}, {last_game.year}"
today = pd.Timestamp.today()
published = f"{today:%B} {today.day}, {today.year}"
data_pulled = L.snapshot_date("fielding_plays").strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
first_season, last_season = int(dfc["year"].min()), int(dfc["year"].max())
n_plays = f"{len(dfc):,}"
n_players = f"{dfc['player_code'].nunique():,}"
n_f_rows = f"{len(f_q):,}"
n_f_players = f"{f_q['player_code'].nunique():,}"
n_c_rows = f"{len(c_q):,}"
n_c_catchers = f"{c_q['player_code'].nunique():,}"


def spread_summary(dist):
    low, mlb = dist.iloc[0], dist[dist["level"] == "mlb"].iloc[0]
    return (low["level_label"], num(low["spread_80"]), num(mlb["spread_80"]),
            f"{low['spread_80'] / mlb['spread_80']:.1f}", f"{low['median_opportunities']:,.0f}",
            f"{mlb['median_opportunities']:,.0f}")


(f_low_label, f_low_spread, f_mlb_spread, f_spread_ratio,
 f_low_opps, f_mlb_opps) = spread_summary(f_dist)
(c_low_label, c_low_spread, c_mlb_spread, c_spread_ratio,
 c_low_opps, c_mlb_opps) = spread_summary(c_dist)


def slope_summary(models):
    return (num(models["slope"].min()), num(models["slope"].max()),
            models["slope"].mean(), models["z_slope"].mean())


f_slope_lo, f_slope_hi, f_slope_avg, f_z_avg = slope_summary(f_models)
c_slope_lo, c_slope_hi, c_slope_avg, c_z_avg = slope_summary(c_models)
f_keep_pct, c_keep_pct = pct(f_slope_avg), pct(c_slope_avg)
f_keep_of_10, c_keep_of_10 = f"{f_slope_avg * 10:.0f}", f"{c_slope_avg * 10:.0f}"


def persistence_summary(pers):
    p = pers.set_index("starting_group")
    return (pct(p.loc["Top 20%", "finished_above_average"]), pct(p.loc["Bottom 20%", "finished_above_average"]),
            pct(p.loc["Top 20%", "finished_in_top_20"]), pct(p.loc["Bottom 20%", "finished_in_top_20"]))


f_top_above, f_bottom_above, f_top_top, f_bottom_top = persistence_summary(f_pers)
c_top_above, c_bottom_above, c_top_top, c_bottom_top = persistence_summary(c_pers)
t_top_above, t_bottom_above, _, _ = persistence_summary(t_pers)


def compare(a, b, tol=0.05, more="more than", less="less than", same="about the same as"):
    return more if a > b + tol else less if a < b - tol else same


def top_bottom_gap(pers):
    p = pers.set_index("starting_group")["finished_above_average"]
    return p["Top 20%"] - p["Bottom 20%"]


t_slope_avg = t_models["slope"].mean()
throw_vs_frame_carry = compare(t_slope_avg, c_slope_avg)
throw_vs_frame_rank = compare(top_bottom_gap(t_pers), top_bottom_gap(c_pers),
                              more="better than", less="less well than", same="about as well as")


def cohort_summary(cohort):
    above = cohort[cohort["current_mlb_percentile"] > 0.5]
    share = (above["average_minor_percentile"] > 0.5).mean()
    r = cohort["average_minor_percentile"].corr(cohort["current_mlb_percentile"])
    return len(cohort), len(above), pct(share), num(r)


f_cohort_n, f_above_n, f_above_share, f_cohort_r = cohort_summary(f_cohort)
c_cohort_n, c_above_n, c_above_share, c_cohort_r = cohort_summary(c_cohort)
```

## Project Summary

::: {.lead}
A player's defensive numbers shrink with every promotion, but where they rank
among their peers holds up. Good defenders in the minors usually become good
defenders in the majors.
:::

::: {.key-stats}
- **`{python} f"{f_slope_avg:.2f}"`** runs: a one-run advantage in FRV/100 at one
  level corresponds to approximately a `{python} f"{f_slope_avg:.2f}"`-run
  advantage at the next level, on average (`{python} f"{c_slope_avg:.2f}"` for
  catcher framing).
- **`{python} f_top_above`** of top-20% position players stay above average after moving
  up (`{python} c_top_above` of top-20% framers).
- **`{python} f_above_share`** of today's above-average MLB position players were above
  average in the minors (`{python} c_above_share` of framers).
- **`{python} share_avg`** of the difference in catchers' season value comes
  from throwing, with framing the rest.
:::

## Introduction

When a player moves up a level, how much of their defensive value comes with them?
This report answers that using SFG
defensive run value from rookie ball through MLB.

**Project Questions:**

1. How do defensive numbers change as players move up the ladder?
2. How much of a player's defense at one level shows up at the next?
3. How do catching skills translate across levels?

**How to read the numbers:**

- **Runs saved per 100 chances** measures a player's defense. 0 is average,
  positive is better than average, negative is worse. For position players a chance is
  a ball in play they could make a play on; for catchers chances are called pitches and
  basestealing throwing opportunities.

- **Rank among peers** compares a player only with others at the same level,
  in the same season, at the same position. A player at
  80% ranks ahead of 80% of their peers.

## Position Players

### Rookie-ball numbers swing much more

```{python}
L.plot_level_spread(f_q, "The range of fielding numbers narrows at every level",
                    "Runs saved per 100 chances")
```

Rookie-ball fielding numbers are spread much wider than MLB numbers. The range
covering most players (the middle 80%) is `{python} f_spread_ratio` times as
wide in `{python} f_low_label` as it is in MLB. Players get fewer chances in
rookie ball, talent is more uneven and tracking systems are less reliable, so big numbers in either direction
are more common and "mean" less.

### Only part of a player's edge moves up with them

```{python}
L.plot_carryover(f_models, f"Position players keep about {f_keep_pct} of their edge at each step")
```

When a position player moves up a level, only about `{python} f_keep_pct` of their edge
over an average player shows up at the next level. For every 10 runs above
average at one level, expect roughly `{python} f_keep_of_10` above average at
the next. The pattern holds at every step, from Rookie Ball to Triple-A to MLB.

### Where a player ranks carries forward

```{python}
L.plot_persistence(f_pers, "Higher-ranked position players stay above average more often",
                   "position players")
```

**How to read this chart:** position players are sorted into five groups by where they
ranked among their peers before a promotion, from the bottom 20% on the left to
the top 20% on the right. Each bar shows how many in that group were **above
average at the next level**. If rank meant nothing, every bar would sit near the
50% line, like a coin flip.

Instead, the bars climb from left to right. Position players in the top 20% are above
average after moving up `{python} f_top_above` of the time, while position players in
the bottom 20% get there only `{python} f_bottom_above` of the time. Even though
the raw numbers shrink, a player's rank holds up.

### Do poor position players still move up?

```{python}
L.plot_promotion(f_promo, "moved_up", "Poor position players move up almost as often as good ones",
                 "Share who later reached a higher level", "position players")
L.plot_promotion(f_promo, "reached_mlb", "Better position players reach MLB a little more often",
                 "Share who later reached MLB", "position players")
```

Yes, most of them do. Looking at minor-league seasons through
`{python} promo_last_start` (so every player has had at least two more seasons to
move up), position players who ranked in the bottom 20% at their level still moved up at
least one level `{python} f_promo_bottom` of the time, compared with
`{python} f_promo_top` for the top 20%. `{python} f_mlb_bottom` of bottom-20%
position players eventually reached MLB, compared with `{python} f_mlb_top` of the top
20%.

Defensive performance is associated with promotion rates, but it is not the sole determining factor. 
Players with below-average defense frequently advance to higher levels, where their defensive struggles can persist.

### Today's good MLB position players were good in the minors

```{python}
L.plot_cohort_scatter(f_cohort, f_year, "Minor-league rank lines up with MLB rank", "position player")
```

Looking back at `{python} f_year` MLB position players who came up through the minors
recently, `{python} f_above_share` of the above-average ones were also above
average in the minors. A good minor-league track record doesn't guarantee a
good MLB defender, but it improves the odds.

The six best and six worst of those MLB position players this season, and how they
ranked at each stop on the way up:

```{python}
L.plot_journeys(f_cohort, f_minors, f_year, "Position player paths to MLB")
```

### Age: position players keep pace until their late 20s

```{python}
prof = f_age_profile.set_index("age")
# Ages where most seasons are in rookie ball swing the most; leave them out
# when describing the low point and the peak.
rookie_share = (f_age.assign(age_int=np.floor(f_age["age"]).astype(int))
                .groupby("age_int")["level_num"].apply(lambda s: (s <= 2).mean()))
steady = prof[rookie_share.reindex(prof.index) < 0.5]
prof_peak_age = int(steady["rate"].idxmax())
prof_peak = f"{steady['rate'].max():+.2f}"
prof_low_age = int(steady.loc[:prof_peak_age, "rate"].idxmin())
prof_low = f"{steady.loc[prof_low_age, 'rate']:+.2f}"
rookie_ages = [int(a) for a in prof.index if a < steady.index.min()]


def pooled(rows):
    return f"{(rows['rate'] * rows['rows']).sum() / rows['rows'].sum():+.2f}"


late_avg = pooled(prof.loc[prof_peak_age + 1:])
below_zero = prof.index[prof["rate"] < 0]
first_below = int(below_zero.min()) if len(below_zero) else None
L.plot_age_profile(f_age_profile, f"Fielding runs peak at {prof_peak_age}, then fall off")
```

**Runs saved at each age.** First, the plain numbers: the average runs saved per
100 chances for position players at each age, across all levels.

- **Building up:** after a low point at `{python} prof_low_age`
  (`{python} prof_low` runs per 100 chances), fielding runs climb to a peak of
  `{python} prof_peak` at age `{python} prof_peak_age`.
- **Falling off:** from `{python} prof_peak_age + 1` on, the average drops to
  `{python} late_avg`, and by `{python} first_below` the typical position player is
  below zero.
- **The youngest ages** (`{python} rookie_ages[0]`–`{python} rookie_ages[-1]`)
  look strong too, but most of those seasons are in rookie ball, where numbers
  swing the most.

Players of the same age are spread across different levels, so this chart mixes
getting older with who is playing where. The next chart handles that by
comparing each player only with peers at their own level.

```{python}
AGE_SPLIT = 27  # first age of the "older" group quoted in the text


def avg_change(rows):
    return (rows["change"] * rows["pairs"]).sum() / rows["pairs"].sum() * 100


young = f_age_change[f_age_change["age"] < AGE_SPLIT]
older = f_age_change[f_age_change["age"] >= AGE_SPLIT]
young_change, older_change = f"{avg_change(young):+.1f}", f"{avg_change(older):+.1f}"
age_first, age_last = int(f_age_change["age"].min()), int(f_age_change["age"].max())
L.plot_aging_curve(f_age_change, "Position players hold their rank through their mid-20s, then start to slip")
```

**Keeping pace with peers.** This chart asks how a position player's **rank among their
peers** changes from one season to the next as they get older. Because rank is measured against
players at the same level, players can be followed even when they move up.
Each bar is the typical change for an average position player at that age. Above zero
means they gained ground on their peers over the next season; below zero means
they lost ground.

- **Up to `{python} AGE_SPLIT - 1`:** position players hold or slightly gain ground,
  about `{python} young_change` rank points a season on average.
- **From `{python} AGE_SPLIT`:** they tend to slip, about
  `{python} older_change` points a season, with the biggest drops in the early
  30s.

The lines on each bar show how uncertain that single age is, and most of them
cross zero. The pattern across ages is more reliable than any one bar.

### Position: players grade worse at harder spots

```{python}

L.styled_boxplot(ax, [qp.loc[qp["position_label"] == p, "sfg_frv_per_100"].clip(p01, p99)
                      for p in L.POSITION_LABEL_ORDER],
                 L.POSITION_LABEL_ORDER, [L.ACCENT] * len(L.POSITION_LABEL_ORDER), alpha=0.55)

order = ["Toward a harder position", "Toward an easier position"]
x = np.arange(len(order))
w = 0.32

           ylabel="Average rank among peers")

```

**Same player, two positions.** When a player played two positions in the same
season and at the same level, they graded worse at the harder position
`{python} harder_worse` of the time. The biggest gap was between
`{python} big_pair[0]` and `{python} big_pair[1]`.

**Changing positions.** Players who moved to an easier position ranked about
`{python} easier_change` points higher the next season. Players who moved to a
harder position ranked about `{python} harder_change` points lower. 

### Position player takeaways

- Rookie-ball fielding numbers swing widely, so judge players against their
  peers at that level.
- Expect about `{python} f_keep_pct` of a position player's edge to carry to the next
  level.
- Rank carries forward: top-20% position players usually stay above average after
  moving up.
- Poor position players still get promoted most of the time, so their defensive
  problems move up with them.
- Position players keep pace with their peers through their mid-20s and start to
  slip from their late 20s.
- Position matters: expect a player's grade to drop at a harder position and
  rise at an easier one.

## Catchers

Catchers generate most of their defensive value differently from other position players, 
primarily through **framing** and **throwing**. Throwing data covers 2016–2026 from Low-A to MLB.

### Framing matters most, but throwing counts too

```{python}
L.plot_value_split(split, f"Framing separates catchers by about {frame_throw_ratio:.1f}× as many runs as throwing")
```

Framing happens on every pitch and throwing only on steal attempts, and over a
season framing makes the bigger difference. A good framer (one standard
deviation above average) saves about `{python} num(mlb_split["framing_sd"], 1)`
runs a season in MLB, and a good thrower about
`{python} num(mlb_split["throwing_sd"], 1)`. Across levels, throwing accounts for
`{python} share_lo`–`{python} share_hi` of the spread in catchers' combined value,
with framing the rest.

- **They're separate skills.** A catcher's framing and throwing runs are barely
  related (correlations of `{python} corr_lo` to `{python} corr_hi` by level), so
  a good framer isn't necessarily a good thrower. Each needs its own look.

### Framing: the rank travels even when the number doesn't

As with position players, framing numbers swing much more in rookie ball (the spread is
`{python} c_spread_ratio` times as wide in `{python} c_low_label` as in MLB), and
a catcher keeps only about `{python} c_keep_pct` of their framing edge when they
move up a level. The Run Value Translator below covers the numbers for any pair of
levels. What stands out for catchers is how well **framing rank** holds up:

```{python}
L.plot_persistence(c_pers, "Higher-ranked framers stay above average more often", "catchers")
```

Catchers in the top 20% at their level are above average framers at the next
level `{python} c_top_above` of the time, and those in the bottom 20% only
`{python} c_bottom_above` of the time. That's a wider gap than for position players
(`{python} f_top_above` against `{python} f_bottom_above`), making framing rank
one of the steadiest signals in this report. It shows at the top too:
`{python} c_above_share` of today's above-average MLB framers were above-average
framers in the minors.

### Caught-stealing rates across levels

```{python}
cs_level = L.caught_stealing_by_level(throws)
cs_season = L.caught_stealing_by_season(throws)
cs2 = cs_level[cs_level["attempted_base"] == "2B"].set_index("level_label")["caught_rate"]
cs3 = cs_level[cs_level["attempted_base"] == "3B"].set_index("level_label")["caught_rate"]
cs_all = cs_level.groupby("level_label").apply(
    lambda g: (g["caught_rate"] * g["attempts"]).sum() / g["attempts"].sum(), include_groups=False)
third_share = (throws.loc[throws["year"] >= L.CURRENT_RULES_FROM, "attempted_base"] == "3B").mean()


def era_rate(years, minors):
    d = cs_season[cs_season["year"].isin(years) & ((cs_season["level_label"] != "MLB") == minors)]
    return (d["caught_rate"] * d["attempts"]).sum() / d["attempts"].sum()


pre_minors, pre_mlb = era_rate(range(2016, 2020), True), era_rate(range(2016, 2020), False)
odd_minors = era_rate([2021, 2022], True)
now_minors, now_mlb = era_rate(range(L.CURRENT_RULES_FROM, 2100), True), era_rate(range(L.CURRENT_RULES_FROM, 2100), False)
L.plot_cs_by_level(cs_level, "Runners are caught at about the same rate at every level")
```

Since `{python} L.CURRENT_RULES_FROM`, when MLB adopted the running-game rules
already in use in the minors (bigger bases and limits on pickoffs), runners have
been caught about as often at every level: `{python} pct(cs_all.min())`–`{python} pct(cs_all.max())`
of attempts.

- **Steals of second are caught far more often than steals of third:**
  `{python} pct(cs2.min())`–`{python} pct(cs2.max())` against
  `{python} pct(cs3.min())`–`{python} pct(cs3.max())`. Steals of third are rarer
  (`{python} pct(third_share)` of attempts), likely because runners are more cautious 
  when attempting a steal of third.
- **The level doesn't change the odds much,** even though pop times get quicker
  higher up (see below), suggesting runners may be more selective, 
  attempting them only when success is more likely.

```{python}
L.plot_cs_by_season(cs_season, "The running game changed with the rules")
```

Over time, caught-stealing rates fell. Before 2020, minor-league runners were
caught `{python} pct(pre_minors)` of the time and MLB runners
`{python} pct(pre_mlb)`; since `{python} L.CURRENT_RULES_FROM` it's
`{python} pct(now_minors)` in the minors and `{python} pct(now_mlb)` in MLB. The
2021–2022 minor-league seasons, when the new rules were being tested, show
unusually low rates (`{python} pct(odd_minors)`); treat those two seasons with
care, since they may partly reflect how those games were recorded. Comparisons
between levels in this section use `{python} L.CURRENT_RULES_FROM` and later.

### What decides a Successful Steal

```{python}
L.plot_caught_stealing_grid(cs_grid, "The catcher's pop time and the pitcher's delivery both decide a steal")
```

Each cell shows how often runners were caught stealing second, by the catcher's
pop time (across) and the pitcher's time to the plate (down). A fast pop behind
a quick pitcher throws out `{python} pct(grid_best)` of runners; a slow pop
behind a slow pitcher, `{python} pct(grid_worst)`.

Looking at the catcher's pop time and arm strength, the pitcher's delivery time
and the runner's speed together on the same attempts, a typical difference in
each moves the caught-stealing rate by:

- **Pitcher's time to the plate:** about `{python} f"{steal_fx['ttp_sd']:.0f}"`
  points for `{python} f"{steal_fx['ttp_sd_seconds']:.2f}"` s quicker, the biggest
  of the four.
- **Runner speed:** about `{python} f"{abs(steal_fx['speed_sd']):.0f}"` points
  for a runner `{python} f"{steal_fx['speed_sd_fts']:.1f}"` ft/s faster (in the
  runner's favor).
- **Catcher's pop time:** about `{python} f"{steal_fx['pop_sd']:.0f}"` points for
  `{python} f"{steal_fx['pop_sd_seconds']:.2f}"` s faster, or
  `{python} f"{steal_fx['pop_tenth']:.0f}"` points per tenth of a second.
- **Catcher's arm strength:** about `{python} f"{steal_fx['arm_sd']:.0f}"` points
  for a throw `{python} f"{steal_fx['arm_sd_mph']:.1f}"` mph harder, or about
  `{python} f"{steal_fx['arm_mph']:.1f}"` points per mph.

```{python}
L.plot_cs_by_arm(cs_arm, "A stronger arm throws out more runners")
```

Arm strength and pop time are the two parts the catcher controls, and they're
related but not the same thing (correlation `{python} num(steal_fx["arm_pop_corr"])`).
Pop time also includes the transfer and footwork, so a catcher with a lighter arm
can make up some ground with a quick release, and a strong arm can be wasted by a
slow one. On the same throws, each is worth about the same. Catchers with the
weakest arms throw out `{python} pct(cs_arm["caught_rate"].iloc[0])` of runners,
against `{python} pct(cs_arm["caught_rate"].iloc[-1])` for the strongest. Even so,
the pitcher's delivery matters at least as much as either.

### Part of a catcher's throwing value belongs to the pitcher

```{python}
L.plot_delivery_effect(delivery, "Same pop time, very different throwing value")
```

To isolate the pitcher's part, this compares throws with nearly the same pop
time (1.80–1.90 s). Behind quick-to-the-plate pitchers, catchers earn
`{python} f"{delivery_quick * 100:+.1f}"` throwing runs per 100 attempts; behind
slow ones, `{python} f"{delivery_slow * 100:+.1f}"`. The catcher's pop time was
about the same; the pitcher's delivery made most of the difference.

So a catcher's throwing runs partly reflect the staff they catch. When comparing
catchers' throwing, check the time to the plate of the pitchers they worked with,
and lean on pop time for the catcher's own part.

### Throwing up the ladder

```{python}
L.plot_carryover(t_models, f"Catchers keep about {t_keep_pct} of their throwing edge at each step")
```

A catcher keeps about `{python} t_keep_pct` of their throwing edge at each step
up, `{python} throw_vs_frame_carry` the `{python} c_keep_pct` they keep for
framing. Throwing rank holds up `{python} throw_vs_frame_rank` framing rank:
top-20% throwers are above average at the next level `{python} t_top_above` of
the time, against `{python} t_bottom_above` for the bottom 20% (for framing,
`{python} c_top_above` against `{python} c_bottom_above`). A catcher also gets a
new pitching staff at every level, which moves their throwing numbers.

- **Pop time gets quicker up the ladder.** The typical catcher's pop time goes
  from `{python} f"{pop_low:.2f}"` s in `{python} pop_low_label` to
  `{python} f"{pop_mlb:.2f}"` s in MLB, while runners are caught about
  `{python} pct(cs_rate_all)` of the time at every level.
- **Pop time travels better than throwing value.** For the
  `{python} pop_carry_n` catchers with tracked throws at two neighbouring levels,
  their pop time at the higher level kept about `{python} pct(pop_carry_slope)`
  of its difference from average, against `{python} t_keep_pct` for throwing
  value. That makes pop time a steadier read on a catcher's arm than the
  throwing value.

### Who moves up

```{python}
L.plot_promotion_compare(c_promo, t_promo, "Framing and throwing both help a catcher move up")
```

Catchers who rank well at either skill are more likely to move up. By framing,
the top 20% moved up `{python} c_promo_top` of the time against
`{python} c_promo_bottom` for the bottom 20%. By throwing, it was
`{python} t_promo_top` against `{python} t_promo_bottom`. Framing also shows in
who reaches MLB: `{python} c_mlb_top` of top-20% framers got there, against
`{python} c_mlb_bottom` of the bottom 20%.

### Catcher takeaways

- Framing separates catchers by about `{python} f"{frame_throw_ratio:.1f}"`×
  as many runs as throwing over a season, but the two are separate skills. Look
  at both.
- Framing rank is one of the steadiest signals in this report: good framers
  usually stay good as they climb.
- The pitcher's time to the plate moves steal outcomes at least as much as pop
  time does, and it shows up in a catcher's throwing runs. Judge a catcher's arm
  by pop time and in the context of their staff.
- Pop time is a steadier read on a catcher's arm than the throwing value: it
  gets quicker up the ladder and carries better from level to level.

## Run Value Translator

If a player saves X runs per 100 chances at one level, what should we expect at
a higher level? And what if a position player moves to the position next door? This
section answers both, using players who actually made the move.

### Moving up a level

These grids cover any pair of levels, not just the next step up. They use players
who played at both levels and compare their full record at each.

```{python}
def tr_row(table, a, b):
    return table[(table["from"] == a) & (table["to"] == b)].iloc[0]


def translate(row, value):
    return row["intercept"] + row["slope"] * value


ex_f = tr_row(f_tr, "Low-A", "Double-A")
ex_f_in, ex_f_out = 3.0, translate(ex_f, 3.0)
ex_c = tr_row(c_tr, "Triple-A", "MLB")
ex_c_in, ex_c_out = 0.3, translate(ex_c, 0.3)
ex_t = tr_row(t_tr, "Double-A", "Triple-A")
ex_t_in, ex_t_out = 5.0, translate(ex_t, 5.0)
dsl_aa_f = tr_row(f_tr, "ROK DSL", "Double-A")
dsl_aa_c = tr_row(c_tr, "ROK DSL", "Double-A")
full_season = f_tr[(f_tr["from_num"] >= 3) & f_tr["slope"].notna()]
fs_lo, fs_hi = pct(full_season["slope"].min()), pct(full_season["slope"].max())
pos_cells = sum(int(t["slope"].notna().sum()) for t in f_tr_by_pos.values())
pos_cells_total = sum(len(t) for t in f_tr_by_pos.values())
L.plot_translation_grid(f_tr, "Position players: how much of a player's edge carries to each higher level",
                        "Share of runs saved above average that shows up at the higher level (all positions)")
```

```{python}
L.plot_translation_grid(c_tr, "Catcher framing: how much of the edge carries to each higher level",
                        "Share of framing runs above average that shows up at the higher level")
```

```{python}
L.plot_translation_grid(t_tr, "Catcher throwing: how much of the edge carries to each higher level",
                        "Share of throwing runs above average that shows up at the higher level (Low-A and up)",
                        levels=L.LEVEL_LABEL_ORDER[2:])
```

**How to read the grids:** find the level a player is at now on the left, then
the level you're projecting to along the top. A cell reading 30% means a player
who is 10 runs per 100 above average should be expected to be about 3 above
average at that level. Grey cells don't have enough players who played at both
levels to give a reliable answer.

- **Between full-season levels** (Low-A and up), position players keep about
  `{python} fs_lo`–`{python} fs_hi` of their edge from one level to any higher
  one. For example, a position player at `{python} f"{ex_f_in:+.1f}"` in Low-A projects to
  about `{python} f"{ex_f_out:+.1f}"` in Double-A.
- **For catchers,** a framer at `{python} f"{ex_c_in:+.1f}"` in Triple-A projects to
  about `{python} f"{ex_c_out:+.2f}"` in MLB, and a thrower at
  `{python} f"{ex_t_in:+.0f}"` runs per 100 steal attempts in Double-A projects to
  about `{python} f"{ex_t_out:+.1f}"` in Triple-A.
- **Rookie-ball numbers barely translate.** Only
  `{python} int(dsl_aa_f["players"])` position players in the data played at both ROK DSL and
  Double-A, too few to say anything. For the `{python} int(dsl_aa_c["players"])`
  catchers who did, DSL framing provided essentially no information about their Double-A
  framing.
- **By position:** the calculator below can also translate one position at a
  time. Splitting by position leaves fewer players per cell, so only
  `{python} pos_cells` of the `{python} pos_cells_total` position-and-level
  combinations have enough players to translate.

### Moving down a level

```{python}
ud = up_down.set_index(["group", "direction"])


def ud_val(group, direction, col):
    return ud.loc[(group, direction), col]


f_down_steps = ud_val("Position players", "down", "steps")
f_down_mlb = f_down_steps.get("MLB → Triple-A", 0)
f_down_n = int(ud_val("Position players", "down", "moves"))
c_down_n = int(ud_val("Catcher framing", "down", "moves"))
L.plot_up_down(up_down, "A player's edge carries about as well going down as going up")
```

The same check works in reverse, using players who were sent down a level
(`{python} f_down_n` position player moves, `{python} f_down_mlb` of them from MLB to
Triple-A, and `{python} c_down_n` catcher framing moves). To compare fairly, the
chart measures each player against their peers at each level, because the spread
of raw numbers is wider at lower levels.

- **Catchers keep about the same share either way:** about
  `{python} pct(ud_val("Catcher framing", "up", "z_slope"))` of their framing edge
  going up and `{python} pct(ud_val("Catcher framing", "down", "z_slope"))` going
  down, and about `{python} pct(ud_val("Catcher throwing", "up", "z_slope"))` and
  `{python} pct(ud_val("Catcher throwing", "down", "z_slope"))` for throwing.
- **Position players keep a little less going down** (`{python} pct(ud_val("Position players", "down", "z_slope"))`
  against `{python} pct(ud_val("Position players", "up", "z_slope"))`), on a smaller
  sample made up mostly of players sent down from MLB.
- **Good defenders stay good after a demotion.** Catchers who were top-20% framers
  before being sent down were above average at the lower level
  `{python} pct(ud_val("Catcher framing", "down", "top_above"))` of the time.

If facing tougher competition were what shrinks a player's edge, players moving
down would keep more of theirs. They keep about the same share (position players even a
little less). That points to the main reason the edge shrinks after any move:
only about a third of one season's number reflects lasting skill, and the rest
doesn't repeat, whichever direction the player goes. So a translation should
pull a number toward average by about the same amount up or down the ladder.

### Switching to a neighbouring position

```{python}
ok_swaps = swaps[swaps["slope"].notna()].copy()
ok_swaps["change"] = ok_swaps["mean_to"] - ok_swaps["mean_from"]  # same players, new spot minus old
lines = ["| Switch | Players | Same players' change | Edge that carries over |",
         "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
for r in ok_swaps.itertuples():
    lines.append(f"| {r[1]} → {r[2]} | {r.players} | {r.change:+.1f} | {r.slope:.0%} |")
from IPython.display import Markdown
too_few_swaps = swaps[swaps["slope"].isna()].drop_duplicates("players")
def swap_gap(frm, to):
    rows = ok_swaps[ok_swaps["from"].isin(frm) & (ok_swaps["to"] == to)]
    return f"{abs((rows['change'] * rows['players']).sum() / rows['players'].sum()):.1f}"


gap_cf, gap_ss_3b, gap_ss_2b = swap_gap(["LF", "RF"], "CF"), swap_gap(["3B"], "SS"), swap_gap(["2B"], "SS")
n_1b_2b = int(swaps.loc[(swaps["from"] == "1B") & (swaps["to"] == "2B"), "players"].iloc[0])
Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

This uses players who qualified at two neighbouring positions in the same season
and level, so the player and the competition are the same and only the position
changes. "Same players' change" is how much better or worse those players did at
the new spot, in runs per 100 chances. "Edge that carries over" is how much of a
player's advantage over their peers at the old spot shows up at the new one.

- **The harder spot costs runs.** The same players average about
  `{python} gap_cf` runs per 100 chances less in CF than in the corners and
  `{python} gap_ss_3b` less at SS than at 3B. The step from 2B to SS is smaller,
  about `{python} gap_ss_2b`.
- **Some of the edge carries over.** A position player above average at one spot keeps
  part of that edge at the neighbouring one, but less than half.
- **1B ↔ 2B:** only `{python} n_1b_2b` players played both in the same season
  and level, too few to translate.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
### Try it: translate a number

```{python}
import json
from IPython.display import HTML


def fits_json(table, key=lambda r: f"{int(r.from_num)}-{int(r.to_num)}"):
    return {key(r): {
                "players": int(r.players),
                "slope": None if np.isnan(r.slope) else round(float(r.slope), 4),
                "intercept": None if np.isnan(r.intercept) else round(float(r.intercept), 4),
                "sd": None if np.isnan(r.resid_sd) else round(float(r.resid_sd), 4)}
            for r in table.itertuples()}


neighbours = {}
for a, b in L.ADJACENT_POSITIONS:
    la, lb = L.POSITION_LABELS[a], L.POSITION_LABELS[b]
    neighbours.setdefault(la, []).append(lb)
    neighbours.setdefault(lb, []).append(la)
neighbours = {p: neighbours[p] for p in L.POSITION_LABEL_ORDER if p in neighbours}

translator_data = {
    "levels": LEVEL_LABEL_ORDER,
    "groups": {
        "fielders": {
            "unit": "chances", "noun": "position players", "firstLevel": 1,
            "positions": [["ALL", "All positions"]] + [[p, p] for p in L.POSITION_LABEL_ORDER],
            "fits": {"ALL": fits_json(f_tr), **{p: fits_json(t) for p, t in f_tr_by_pos.items()}},
            "default": {"from": 3, "to": 5, "value": 2.0, "step": 0.5}},
        "framing": {
            "unit": "called pitches", "noun": "catchers", "firstLevel": 1,
            "fits": {"ALL": fits_json(c_tr)},
            "default": {"from": 6, "to": 7, "value": 0.2, "step": 0.05}},
        "throwing": {
            "unit": "steal attempts", "noun": "catchers", "firstLevel": 3,
            "fits": {"ALL": fits_json(t_tr)},
            "default": {"from": 5, "to": 6, "value": 5.0, "step": 1}},
    },
    "swaps": {
        "neighbours": neighbours,
        "fits": fits_json(swaps, key=lambda r: f"{r[1]}>{r[2]}"),
        "default": {"from": "SS", "to": "3B"},
    },
}
HTML((ARTICLE_DIR / "translator.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
     .replace("__TRANSLATOR_DATA__", json.dumps(translator_data)))
```

## What This Means for Player Development

- **Look at rank, not the raw number.** Where a player ranks among their peers
  tells you more about the next level than their runs-saved total does.
- **Expect big numbers to come down.** A player well above average at one
  level will usually still be above average at the next, but by less.
- **Be careful with rookie-ball numbers.** They swing the most, and they
  barely translate to the upper levels.
- **Minor-league framing is a strong signal.** Catchers who frame well in the
  minors usually keep framing well.
- **Judge a catcher's arm by pop time, in the context of their staff.** A
  catcher's throwing runs rise and fall with how quickly their pitchers get the
  ball to the plate.
- **Don't expect promotions to fix defense.** Poor position players keep moving up, so
  work on defense in the lower levels, while players are still gaining ground.
- **Position changes show up quickly.** Expect a player's grade to drop at a
  harder position and rise at an easier one.

## Data and Methods

### Caveats

- **Who's included.** A position player needs at least
  `{python} L.FIELDING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES` chances at one position in a season at
  a level, and a catcher needs at least `{python} L.FRAMING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES`
  called pitches. These cutoffs make sure there's enough data to include a
  player-season. They don't make one season's number reliable on its own.
- **The MLB comparisons only look back.** They include players who reached
  MLB with a complete minor-league record. They say nothing about players who
  were released, stalled, or never reached the cutoffs, and they use a single
  season (`{python} f_year`), not full careers.
- **Not cause and effect.** The age and position results show patterns, not
  causes. For example, a team may move a player to an easier position because
  they were already losing range.
- **Framing only for catchers.** The framing results don't account for the
  pitching staff, umpires, or changes in a catcher's receiving technique.
- **Throwing tracking is thin.** Throwing covers
  `{python} throw_first_year`–`{python} throw_last_year`, Low-A to MLB (the source
  has one combined rookie code, which can't be split into DSL and Complex League
  like the rest of this report, so rookie ball is left out). Pop time is tracked
  on only `{python} pct(throws["catcher_pop_time"].notna().mean())` of steal
  attempts (`{python} pop_year_text`), arm strength on
  `{python} pct(throws["arm_strength"].notna().mean())` and the pitcher's time to
  the plate on `{python} pct(throws["ttp"].notna().mean())`, so the steal model and
  grid rest on a few thousand attempts.
- **The Position Players section leaves out catchers.** Catchers never reach the
  `{python} L.FIELDING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES`-chance fielding cutoff, so that section
  covers the other seven positions, and catchers get their own section.

### Data

The position player data covers `{python} n_plays` modeled plays by
`{python} n_players` players from `{python} first_season` to
`{python} last_season`. After the cutoff, that leaves `{python} n_f_rows`
player-season-level-position rows (`{python} n_f_players` players). The framing
data has `{python} n_c_rows` qualifying catcher-season-level rows
(`{python} n_c_catchers` catchers).

- **Sources:** `queries/play_by_play.sql` (fielding plays),
  `queries/framing_level_agg.sql` (framing, aggregated in BigQuery from the
  pitch-level `frv-catching` table), `queries/catcher_throwing.sql` (catcher
  throwing on stolen-base attempts, from the `xsb` table with level and season
  added from the catcher-throw play-by-play), and birth dates from
  `tblPlayer_Pro`.
- **Levels**, in order: ROK DSL, Complex League, Low-A, High-A, Double-A,
  Triple-A, MLB. The two rookie levels are kept separate because they are
  different competitive and tracking environments.

### Definitions

- **FRV/100** ("runs saved per 100 chances"): SFG-modeled defensive run value
  (`-runs_plus_minus`) summed over a player-season at a level and divided by
  opportunities, times 100. Position player opportunities are modeled plays; framing
  opportunities are called pitches (`ball_called` / `strike_called`).
- **Percentile** ("rank among peers"): the percentile rank of FRV/100 within
  the same season and level (and, for position players, position).
- **Spread**: the 90th minus the 10th percentile of FRV/100 at a level. For
  position players it goes from `{python} f_low_spread` in `{python} f_low_label` to
  `{python} f_mlb_spread` in MLB. For framing it goes from `{python} c_low_spread`
  to `{python} c_mlb_spread`. The median qualified player has
  `{python} f_low_opps` fielding chances in `{python} f_low_label` against
  `{python} f_mlb_opps` in MLB, and a catcher sees `{python} c_low_opps` called
  pitches against `{python} c_mlb_opps`, which is part of why the lower levels
  are noisier.

### How reliable are these numbers?

The rates in this report (fielding runs per 100 chances, framing runs per 100
called pitches, throwing runs per 100 steal attempts) mix two things: the
player's real skill and chance. Reliability is the share that reflects the
player. At 50%, a rate is half signal and half noise; the more chances behind
it, the higher it gets.

```{python}
f_rel_pts = L.split_half_points(dfc, ["player_code", "year", "level", "position"], "sfg_rv",
                                ["year", "level", "position"], [10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200])
c_rel_pts = L.split_half_points_from_sums(
    L.cached_query("framing_split_half", (L.QUERY_DIR / "framing_split_half.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8"),
                   refresh).rename(columns={"catcher_sfg_id": "player_code"}),
    ["year", "level"])
t_rel_pts = L.split_half_points(throws, ["player_code", "year", "level"], "throw_runs", ["year", "level"],
                                [5, 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 80])

rel_rows = []
for label, unit, pts, q, cutoff, rows, keys, peers in [
    ("Fielding FRV/100", "chances", f_rel_pts, f_q, L.FIELDING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES, f_agg,
     ["player_code", "position"], ["year", "level", "position"]),
    ("Framing runs/100 pitches", "called pitches", c_rel_pts, c_q, L.FRAMING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES, c_agg,
     ["player_code"], ["year", "level"]),
    ("Throwing runs/100 attempts", "steal attempts", t_rel_pts, t_q, L.THROWING_MIN_ATTEMPTS, t_all,
     ["player_code"], ["year", "level"]),
]:
    n50, ext50 = L.n_for_reliability(pts, 0.5)
    n70, ext70 = L.n_for_reliability(pts, 0.7)
    typical = q["opportunities"].median()
    yoy_r, yoy_n = L.season_to_season(rows, keys, peers, cutoff)
    rel_rows.append({"label": label, "unit": unit, "points": pts, "typical": typical,
                     "n50": n50, "ext50": ext50, "n70": n70, "ext70": ext70, "cutoff": cutoff,
                     "rel_cutoff": float(L.reliability_at(pts, cutoff)),
                     "rel_typical": float(L.reliability_at(pts, typical)), "yoy": yoy_r, "yoy_n": yoy_n})
rel = {r["label"].split()[0].lower(): r for r in rel_rows}

L.plot_reliability(rel_rows, "How many chances before a rate mostly reflects the player")
```

```{python}
def n_text(n, extrapolated):
    return f"{n:,.0f}{'*' if extrapolated else ''}"


lines = ["| Measure | 50% reliable at | 70% reliable at | At the cutoff | Typical qualifying season | Next season (r) |",
         "|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for r in rel_rows:
    lines.append(f"| {r['label']} | {n_text(r['n50'], r['ext50'])} {r['unit']} | "
                 f"{n_text(r['n70'], r['ext70'])} | {r['rel_cutoff']:.0%} ({r['cutoff']:,}) | "
                 f"{r['rel_typical']:.0%} ({r['typical']:,.0f}) | {r['yoy']:.2f} |")
Markdown("\n".join(lines) + "\n\n\\* Past the largest sample measurable, so extended (see below).")
```

- **A single season of FRV/100 is mostly noise.** A position player needs about
  `{python} n_text(rel["fielding"]["n50"], rel["fielding"]["ext50"])` chances
  for the rate to be half signal. A typical qualifying season
  (`{python} f"{rel['fielding']['typical']:,.0f}"` chances) is about
  `{python} pct(rel["fielding"]["rel_typical"])` reliable, and the report's
  `{python} L.FIELDING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES`-chance cutoff about
  `{python} pct(rel["fielding"]["rel_cutoff"])`. That's why this report leans on
  rank and on pooled records, and why a single season's number should be pulled
  well toward average before it's used to judge a player.
- **Framing gets enough pitches within a season.** It reaches 50% at about
  `{python} n_text(rel["framing"]["n50"], rel["framing"]["ext50"])` called
  pitches, and a catcher sees far more than that, so a typical season (`{python} f"{rel['framing']['typical']:,.0f}"`
  pitches) is about `{python} pct(rel["framing"]["rel_typical"])` reliable. But it
  repeats less from one season to the next (r = `{python} num(rel["framing"]["yoy"])`)
  than that suggests. Pitches within a season share the same pitching staff,
  umpires and parks, so part of what looks like a catcher's skill within a season
  is their situation, and it changes when the situation does.
- **Throwing is about half signal in a typical season.** It takes about
  `{python} n_text(rel["throwing"]["n50"], rel["throwing"]["ext50"])` steal
  attempts to reach 50%, about as many as a catcher faces in a typical season
  (`{python} f"{rel['throwing']['typical']:,.0f}"`). Pop time, which is measured
  directly on each throw, is a steadier read on the arm (see Catchers).
- **Season to season,** a player's rate (against their peers) correlates
  `{python} num(rel["fielding"]["yoy"])` for fielding,
  `{python} num(rel["framing"]["yoy"])` for framing and
  `{python} num(rel["throwing"]["yoy"])` for throwing. Those are in line with the
  roughly one-third carry-over between levels: most of the shrinking after a move
  is the noise in one season's number washing out.

**How it's measured:** for each sample size, the analysis takes player-seasons with at least
twice that many chances, put their chances in random order, and correlate the
rate over the first half with the rate over the second half across players, each
half measured against peers at the same level and season (and position, for
position players). That correlation is the reliability of a rate based on that many
chances. Values between measured sizes are interpolated. Beyond the largest size with at
least 30 players, the curve is extended from the largest measured point with the
Spearman–Brown formula (marked with *), which assumes the next chances behave
like the earlier ones and may run a little high. Season to season uses each
player's rate against peers in consecutive seasons (same position for position players),
with seasons at several levels combined. The framing split uses
`queries/framing_split_half.sql`, which orders each catcher-season's pitches
randomly in BigQuery.

### How carry-over is measured

For each pair of consecutive stints one level apart (a stint is a player's
season at a level, ordered by its first and last game dates, so a demotion in
the middle of a season isn't mistaken for a promotion), a linear
regression of next-level FRV/100 on current-level FRV/100 is fit separately for each
step up the ladder. The slope measures how differences in observed FRV/100
translate between levels; it's what the charts above show as the "share carried
over". 1.0 would mean a difference carries over in full, and 0 would mean no
relationship. Position player slopes run `{python} f_slope_lo`–`{python} f_slope_hi`
(average `{python} num(f_slope_avg)`), and framing slopes run
`{python} c_slope_lo`–`{python} c_slope_hi` (average `{python} num(c_slope_avg)`).
Steps with fewer than 30 position player pairs or 20 catcher pairs aren't fit.

**Does the narrowing spread explain the drop?** Because each level's spread is
narrower than the one below, a player who keeps exactly the same rank will
still show a smaller raw number. To check, FRV/100 was standardized to a
z-score within each season and level before refitting (orange bars below).

- **Position players:** the average slope barely moves (`{python} num(f_slope_avg)` →
  `{python} num(f_z_avg)`), so nearly all of the drop is real regression.
- **Framing:** the average slope rises (`{python} num(c_slope_avg)` →
  `{python} num(c_z_avg)`), so part of the raw drop reflects the narrowing
  scale. The slopes still stay well below 1.0.

```{python}
L.plot_slopes(f_models, "Position players: raw vs. standardized carry-over slopes")
L.plot_slopes(c_models, "Catcher framing: raw vs. standardized carry-over slopes")
```

**Rank persistence.** The same back-to-back pairs are grouped by their
lower-level percentile (in 20-point bands). For each band, the analysis counts the share
finishing above the 50th percentile and above the 80th percentile at the next
level. Top-20% position players stay in the top 20% `{python} f_top_top` of the time
(bottom-20%: `{python} f_bottom_top`). For catchers it's `{python} c_top_top`
(bottom-20%: `{python} c_bottom_top`).

### MLB comparison group

The comparison group is players in the most recent MLB season
(`{python} f_year`) who qualified at two or more distinct minor-league levels
before their first MLB game and debuted after
`{python} L.MINOR_HISTORY_DEBUT_CUTOFF`. Play-by-play data starts in 2021, so
earlier debuts would have incomplete histories. Minor-league games after the
debut, including rehab assignments, are excluded. That leaves
`{python} f_cohort_n` position players (`{python} f_above_n` above average) and
`{python} c_cohort_n` catchers (`{python} c_above_n` above average). MLB rank
is within position for position players.

The "above average in the minors" share uses each player's average minor-league
percentile. Across everyone in the group, the correlation between average
minor-league percentile and current MLB percentile is modest:
`{python} f_cohort_r` for position players and `{python} c_cohort_r` for catchers. That's
why the article says a strong minor-league record improves the odds rather than
settles the question.

### Run Value Translator

For every pair of levels, the analysis selects players with a qualifying record at both (for
position players, at the same position) whose first game at the higher level came after
their first game at the lower one. Each player's seasons at a level are pooled into one record, which
must meet the usual cutoff (`{python} L.FIELDING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES` chances for
position players, `{python} L.FRAMING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES` called pitches for catchers).
A straight line was then fit to the higher-level rate using the lower-level rate.

- The percentage in each cell is the slope. A projection is intercept + slope ×
  the lower-level rate, so it also reflects any difference in average between
  the two groups.
- Pairs with fewer than `{python} TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["fielders"]` position players
  or `{python} TRANSLATION_MIN_PLAYERS["catchers"]` catchers are left blank. The
  same applies to the by-position translations, which are fit separately for each
  position on players who played that position at both levels.
- **Catcher throwing** uses throwing runs per 100 steal attempts (measured against
  the average attempt at that level and season), with at least
  `{python} L.THROWING_MIN_ATTEMPTS` attempts at each level, Low-A and up.
- **Position switches** use players who qualified at two neighbouring positions
  (1B–2B, 2B–SS, SS–3B, LF–CF, CF–RF) in the same season and level, fitting FRV/100
  at the new position on FRV/100 at the old one, separately in each direction.
  Levels are pooled, so the translation doesn't depend on level.
- The calculator's likely range is the projection ± 1.28 residual standard
  deviations, which covers about 80% of players. Records here pool all seasons at
  a level, so a single season will usually be noisier than that range suggests.
- Fitting each pair directly avoids chaining the step-by-step results, which
  would multiply every step's regression and understate how much carries over
  across several levels.

### Who moves up

For every qualified minor-league season through `{python} promo_last_start`, the
analysis checks whether the player later appeared at a higher level (a stint there that
started after this one did, at any position, with any number of chances) and
whether they appeared in MLB. Going by dates means a player sent down in the
middle of a season isn't counted as moving up because of where they started the
year. Ending in `{python} promo_last_start` gives every player at
least `{python} PROMOTION_WINDOW` more seasons to move up. Seasons after a
player's first MLB season are left out, so veterans sent back to the minors
don't count as "reaching" MLB. Rank is the same within-level percentile used
elsewhere. That leaves `{python} f"{len(f_promo_rows):,}"` position player seasons and
`{python} f"{len(c_promo_rows):,}"` catcher seasons.

This also matters for the rank persistence results. Those only include players
who were promoted, so if poor position players were rarely promoted, the results would
describe a select group. Because most poor position players do move up, that selection
effect is small for position players. It is larger for catchers.

### Catcher throwing

Each row is a stolen-base attempt (steals of second and third) at Low-A to MLB.
The catcher's value is the stolen-base model's `catcher_runs_plus_minus`, which
covers nearly every attempt (the throw model's value only exists on attempts
with a tracked throw, and correlates 0.98 with it where both exist). As with
framing, throwing runs are `-runs_plus_minus`, so positive means runs saved by
the catcher. The model's catcher, pitcher and baserunner values for an attempt
are nearly identical (correlation above 0.99): each is close to the full value
of the attempt rather than a split of it, which is why the pitcher's delivery
shows up in the catcher's number. Pop times outside 1.6–2.4 s, times to the plate outside 1.1–1.8 s
runner speeds outside 22–32 ft/s and arm strengths outside 60–95 mph are treated
as tracking errors and dropped.

- **Framing vs. throwing:** for catcher-seasons at a level with a qualifying
  framing season (`{python} L.FRAMING_MIN_OPPORTUNITIES`+ called pitches) and any
  steal attempts, the standard deviation of season framing runs is compared with
  that of season throwing runs. Throwing's share is its variance over the sum of
  both variances. Throwing's spread includes more noise, since a season has only
  a few dozen attempts.
- **Steal model:** a logistic regression of caught stealing on the catcher's pop
  time and arm strength, the pitcher's time to the plate, runner sprint speed and
  level, on the `{python} f"{steal_n:,}"` steals of second where all four were
  tracked. Arm strength on its own uses the `{python} f"{arm_n:,}"` steals of
  second where it was tracked, split into four equal groups. The
  effects quoted are average marginal effects for one standard deviation. The
  grid uses the `{python} f"{grid_n:,}"` steals of second with both pop time and
  time to the plate tracked; cells with fewer than 50 attempts are left blank.
- **Pitcher effect:** throws with a pop time of 1.80–1.90 s, split into thirds by
  the pitcher's time to the plate.
- **Across levels:** catcher-season-level throwing needs
  `{python} L.THROWING_MIN_ATTEMPTS`+ steal attempts; carry-over and rank
  persistence use the same method as framing, on throwing runs per 100 attempts.
  Pop time carry-over uses catchers with 10+ tracked throws at two neighbouring
  levels (slope `{python} num(pop_carry_slope)`, correlation
  `{python} num(pop_carry_r)`, `{python} pop_carry_n` catchers). Season to season
  at any level, a catcher's average pop time correlates
  `{python} num(pop_repeat_r)` with the next season (`{python} pop_repeat_n`
  catchers with 10+ tracked throws in both).

### Age

**Age** is as of July 1 of the season (whole years).

**Runs saved at each age:** total runs saved divided by total chances for all
qualifying player-seasons at that age, across all levels. This means seasons
with more chances count more. Ages with fewer than 30 player-seasons are left
out, and the band is a 95% bootstrap interval from resampling players. The peak
and low point quoted in the text leave out ages where most seasons are in the
two rookie levels.
Qualifying position players average slightly above zero overall, so the shape matters
more than where the line sits relative to zero.

**Keeping pace with peers:** this chart uses pairs
of consecutive seasons by the same player at the same position, at **any
level** (`{python} f"{len(f_age_pairs):,}"` pairs), so players who move up are
kept. The outcome is the player's percentile within season, level and position
in the second season.

Chaining raw percentile changes would be misleading. Players who qualify in two
seasons in a row were above average the first year and drift back toward the
middle the next, whatever their age. A weighted regression therefore uses
next-season percentile as the outcome, with age (one term per age), the starting percentile
(centered at 50), and whether the player moved up or down a level:

- Each bar is the age term minus 50: the expected change for a player who
  starts at the median and stays at the same level.
- Weights are the harmonic mean of the two seasons' chances. Only ages with at
  least 40 pairs are shown (`{python} age_first`–`{python} age_last`).
- About `{python} pct(f_age_effects["carry"])` of a player's distance from the
  median carries into the next season. Moving up a level costs
  `{python} f"{abs(f_age_effects['moved_up']) * 100:.1f}"` rank points on top of
  that.
- The error bars are 95% bootstrap intervals from resampling players.

Rank is relative to peers who are also aging and moving up, so this shows
whether a position player keeps pace with their competition, not how their absolute
fielding changes. If everyone in a peer group improved at the same rate, none of
them would change rank, so that kind of improvement doesn't show up here.

### Position

- **Position spread:** `{python} widest_pos` has the widest spread
  (`{python} widest_spread`) and `{python} narrowest_pos` the narrowest
  (`{python} narrowest_spread`). Positions are ordered along the traditional
  defensive spectrum: SS, CF, 2B, 3B, RF, LF, 1B.
- **Two positions in one season:** `{python} n_pairs` player-seasons in which a
  player qualified at exactly two positions in the same season and level. The
  harder position graded worse `{python} harder_worse` of the time, by an
  average of `{python} avg_gap` percentile points. The largest gap among
  pairings with 50+ cases was `{python} big_pair[0]` compared with
  `{python} big_pair[1]` (`{python} big_pair_gap` points,
  `{python} big_pair_n` cases).
- **Position changes:** a player's primary position each season is the
  qualified position with the most chances. `{python} n_moves` season-to-season
  changes in primary position were found, and `{python} share_easier` were moves
  toward the easier end of the spectrum.
